Your deck-building decisions are too focused on whether each individual card is locally useful. Build toward a coherent long-term deck plan instead. Before adding a card, identify what the current deck's damage plan, defense plan, scaling, draw/energy needs, and major weaknesses are. Add a card only when it meaningfully fills one of those needs, strengthens an existing synergy, or enables a clear new strategy; otherwise skip it. Do not keep adding generically good cards simply because each one can be justified individually.

In combat, preserve the full-turn sequence you planned. If you plan to use setup followed by defense, do not abandon the defensive part on the next decision unless the game state materially changes. When lethal is not available and an enemy is attacking, avoid preventable HP loss when available block can substantially reduce or fully mitigate that damage and extra damage does not meaningfully change the fight. In particular, do not spend the remaining energy on marginal attacks after already planning to block.

Your deck planning improved this run, but you are still not treating the weaknesses identified in your own deck plan as real priorities. When the deck plan identifies a critical missing role, especially long-term damage scaling, prioritize cards that directly solve that weakness over cards that are merely efficient incremental upgrades. For example, in Act 2 you explicitly identified Strength/scaling as the deck's main missing component, but still chose Sword Boomerang over Spot Weakness. Sword Boomerang only gives more immediate attack damage, while Spot Weakness directly addresses the scaling problem you had already identified. Do not let short-term card quality override the long-term need stated in your own plan.

As the deck becomes more complete, raise the threshold for adding another card. Once damage, defense, draw and AoE are already adequately covered, a card should only beat Skip if it materially solves a named weakness, significantly strengthens an existing synergy, or enables a clear new strategy. A card being somewhat useful is not enough. If the deck plan says the deck is already large or compact and the main weakness is scaling, additions such as Armaments that do not solve that weakness should usually lose to Skip.

Combat sequencing was much better this run. Continue committing to the full-turn sequence and use the cheapest sufficient defensive option. Before spending Apparition, Impervious or other limited defensive resources, calculate the actual incoming damage and the block that the planned sequence will generate. If ordinary block fully mitigates the attack, preserve the stronger limited resource; if ordinary block is insufficient, use the stronger defense rather than taking preventable damage. Base this on the actual mitigation calculation, not simply on whether multiple enemies are attacking.

You are still taking too much unnecessary damage in combat. When enemies are attacking and lethal is not available, first calculate the incoming damage and how much of it can be prevented with the block currently available in your hand. If playing defensive cards can substantially reduce or completely prevent the damage, prioritize that defense unless spending the energy on damage will clearly end the fight or remove a major threat. Do not take preventable HP loss just to deal a small amount of extra damage. At the same time, when enemies are not attacking, do not waste energy on unnecessary block and use the turn to deal damage, set up your deck, or apply useful debuffs.

You also need to continue following encounter-specific strategies that were taught in previous runs rather than treating newer lessons as replacements. For example, against Centurion and Mystic, prioritize killing Centurion before Mystic as previously taught. More generally, consider which enemy is the main threat and follow previously learned target priorities instead of choosing targets only based on immediate damage. Continue sequencing cards correctly as well: apply effects such as Vulnerable before attacks that benefit from them, and play according to the synergies and strengths of the deck you have built.

Your deck is also becoming too large because you are still taking cards that are only individually useful rather than necessary for the build. Commit to the deck's existing strategy and be much more selective with card rewards. Once the deck already has a functioning damage plan, defense, draw/energy and supporting synergy, Skip should be the default unless a new card clearly fills an important missing role or significantly strengthens the existing build. Do not keep adding cards simply because they are decent cards. Avoid unnecessary redundancy and deck dilution, and keep the deck compact enough that its strongest cards and synergies are drawn consistently.

Your combat planning and card selection showed some improvement this run. The deck remained relatively compact at 19 cards, you skipped several unnecessary rewards, and you correctly followed the previously taught strategy of targeting Centurion before Mystic. Continue retaining and applying lessons from all previous runs.

However, your combat damage calculations are still inaccurate. Before approving a turn plan, calculate the actual incoming damage and the effective Block gained after accounting for player debuffs such as Frail. In the Collector fight, your verifier predicted 49 Block against 46 incoming damage on Turn 6, but the actual sequence generated only 36 Block, causing a fatal 10 HP loss when you had 5 HP remaining. A similar underestimation occurred on Turn 5. Do not calculate defense using the cards' printed Block values without accounting for current status effects. Your verifier must critically evaluate the full planned sequence instead of approving it based on incorrect calculations. Playing Impervious earlier in the same turn would not, by itself, have solved this problem.

Your deck-building was more selective, but you still need to distinguish between strengthening an existing synergy and building sufficient damage scaling for longer boss fights. The Fire Breathing and Reckless Charge combination is a legitimate strategy because Reckless Charge generates Dazed cards, but additional copies should only be taken when they meaningfully improve the deck. You ended with three Reckless Charges and three Pommel Strikes, while your long-term scaling remained limited. At the Act 1 Floor 13 shop, you bought Reckless Charge instead of considering Demon Form, despite previously being taught its value. Evaluate whether a card solves an important weakness rather than repeatedly reinforcing an already functional part of the build.

Finally, prioritize survival when approaching dangerous bosses. At the Act 2 Floor 32 campfire, you upgraded Bash while at 57/80 HP instead of resting before the Collector, despite having no potions remaining. Consider whether the additional HP would provide more value than a marginal upgrade, especially when your defense is inconsistent. Your objective is not simply to maximize card efficiency on individual turns, but to preserve enough HP and build sufficient damage scaling to survive and defeat the upcoming boss.

Your cumulative memory and Block calculations have improved. You maintained a compact 20-card deck, selected useful cards such as Demon Form and Disarm, and your combat verifier correctly accounted for Frail in several defensive decisions. Continue applying the lessons from all previous runs.

However, you need to improve your long-term combat planning. During the Act 2 Spheric Guardian fight, you lost approximately 52 HP over a prolonged encounter. Demon Form remained available in your hand for much of the fight but was never played. When facing an enemy with high or recurring Block, evaluate whether investing in scaling early, when survivable, will prevent greater HP losses over future turns. Do not repeatedly play low-impact attacks into Block without a realistic plan for overcoming the enemy's defenses. Balance immediate mitigation with establishing the damage needed to end prolonged fights.

You must also adapt your strategic decisions to your current HP and upcoming encounters. At the Act 2 Floor 19 shop, you had only 34/80 HP but spent your gold on Armaments, Inflame, and card removal rather than considering immediate survival resources such as Essence of Steel. These purchases may provide long-term value, but the priority should shift toward surviving the next dangerous encounter when health is critically low. Evaluate whether a potion, defensive card, safer route, or other immediate resource is more valuable than improving the deck for later fights.

Additionally, consider the complete upcoming route before entering dangerous elites. You entered the Gremlin Leader fight at just 25/80 HP with no potions, leaving very little room for mistakes. Avoid optional high-risk encounters when the current deck and remaining HP cannot reliably survive them, unless their expected reward clearly justifies the danger. Preserve HP throughout the run rather than relying on emergency defense only when near death.

Finally, improve combat threat assessment. Before ending a turn, evaluate current enemy intents, actual incoming damage, available energy, defensive alternatives, and whether killing an enemy removes an immediate threat. Do not waste Block when enemies definitely are not attacking, but treat uncertain intents carefully, especially at low HP. In multi-enemy fights, prioritize enemies according to the threats they pose over the next several turns rather than considering only immediate damage.

Continue maintaining the cumulative lessons from earlier runs while adapting them to the current encounter, deck synergies, and survival requirements.

Run 37 achieved its first Ascension 0 victory, demonstrating effective Strength scaling, selective card rewards, and appropriate healing during critical situations. These are positive behaviors worth retaining.

However, the run exposed an important weakness in recognizing delayed enemy damage. At Act 3 Floor 39, an Exploder remained alive with 14 HP on turn 3. The agent invested in Inflame and Demon Form while its verifier accounted for only 8 displayed incoming damage. The following turn, HP dropped from 47 to 17 and the Exploder disappeared, consistent with its 30-damage detonation.

When fighting enemies with delayed or conditional attacks, such as Exploder, do not rely solely on the currently displayed attack-damage total. Track enemy-specific mechanics and timing, anticipate imminent burst damage, and prioritize eliminating dangerous enemies on earlier turns or preparing sufficient mitigation. In particular, treat an Exploder approaching detonation as an immediate survival threat even if its intent is UNKNOWN.

Continue investing in Strength scaling during genuinely safe setup opportunities, as demonstrated against Donu and Deca, but first ensure that immediate and delayed damage will not put survival at unacceptable risk.
